title: Who, Me? At the Table
subtitle: Six sessions for the ordinary Christian who is sure they are not qualified to disciple anyone
summary: Most believers have quietly decided that discipling other people is a job for pastors, for experts, for the ones who went to seminary and never seem to doubt. This study is six sessions written to that fear, one on one or with two or three, over coffee or a meal. It walks through the twelve who were nobodies, the plain truth that you are not the source of anyone's change, the freedom of being only one step ahead, the honesty of I do not know so let us find out together, the courage to start before you feel ready, and the only requirement that ever actually mattered. The aim is simple. By the last session the reader has stopped waiting to be qualified and has begun walking one real person toward Jesus.
setting: A kitchen table or a coffee shop. One person a step ahead, one person willing to come along.
forWho: The believer who thinks discipling is for pastors and experts, and the one paralyzed by the fear of not knowing enough.
rhythm: Six sessions, forty five minutes, one on one or with two or three, over coffee or a meal.
leaderNote: Aim the whole study at the fear underneath. I am not qualified. Every session, in some form, will try to pry that fear loose, so name it out loud in the first ten minutes and keep coming back to it. The qualification is not expertise. It is a life going somewhere and a willingness to bring one person along. Do not let this stay a discussion. Push the person you are meeting with to name, out loud and early, one actual human being they could walk with, and by session six help them take a first step toward that person. If they finish the study more informed and still on the sidelines, the study failed. Let the reader disciple someone by the end.

sessions.title: The Twelve Were Nobodies
sessions.bigIdea: The first disciple-makers were untrained fishermen with no credentials and no titles, and the one thing that marked them in front of the authorities was not their learning. It was that they had been with Jesus.
sessions.open: When you hear the word discipling, who do you picture doing it? Be honest. Describe the person, and then ask yourself why that person is never you.
sessions.read: Read Acts 4:13. Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus. Remember who is speaking here. This is the council in Jerusalem, the trained religious professionals, looking at two fishermen who were teaching the resurrection with more nerve than the experts could explain.
observe: What two words does Luke use to describe Peter and John? Say them out loud and let them land.
The council was astonished, but they landed on one explanation for the boldness. What was it? Where does the power in the verse come from?
talk: Uneducated and common. Those are the men Jesus spent three years building, and they turned the world over. What does that do to your private belief that you need more training before you could help anyone?

The council could not deny the boldness, but they could explain it. These men had been with Jesus. Not around religion, with the person. How much of your week is spent with him, and how much is spent near the machinery of church?
Name it plainly. What is the specific credential you keep telling yourself you are missing before you could walk with someone? Say it, and then ask whether Peter had it.
sessions.practice: This week, spend fifteen minutes a day simply being with Jesus, a gospel open, no notes, no agenda, just the person. Track whether being with him does more for your confidence than another book about him would.
sessions.send: The council could not tell you had a degree. They could tell you had been with him. That is the only qualification the verse cares about.
sessions.passItOn: Tell one person this week the plain fact that the first disciple-makers were untrained fishermen. Watch their face. The person who most needs to hear that they are not disqualified is often the one you say it to.

sessions.title: You Are Not the Source
sessions.bigIdea: The Spirit does the convincing and the changing. You are a witness, not the power company. That single truth takes the crushing weight off your shoulders, because no one was ever saved by your cleverness and no one is lost by your fumbling.
sessions.open: Have you ever avoided talking about your faith because you were afraid you would mess it up and lose someone? What exactly were you afraid would happen if you got it wrong?
sessions.read: Read John 15:26-27. But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning. Jesus is talking to frightened men on the night before he dies, and he tells them who actually does the heavy lifting.
observe: Two parties bear witness in this passage. Who is the first, and who is the second? Whose witness is named first?
What is the Spirit called here, and what does that title tell you about who is responsible for the truth landing in a person?
talk: The Spirit bears witness, and then you also bear witness. You are the second voice, not the first. If the Spirit is the one who convinces a heart, what pressure can you finally set down tonight?

A witness in a courtroom does not manufacture the evidence. A witness simply says what they saw. What have you actually seen and received from Jesus that you could just report, no theology degree required?

Here is where the fear hides. We act like a person's eternity rests on our performance, which is really a way of making ourselves more central than the Spirit. Where has your fear of failing quietly turned into pride about being the deciding factor?
sessions.practice: This week, before any spiritual conversation, pray one sentence. Spirit, you go first, I will follow. Then just say what you have seen, and leave the results to the one who actually changes people.
sessions.send: You were never the source. You are the witness. Take the weight off your back and put it where it always belonged.
sessions.passItOn: Find one believer this week who is frozen by the fear of saying the wrong thing, and hand them this one line. The Spirit does the converting, you just tell what you saw. Release someone else the way you were released.

sessions.title: One Step Ahead Is Enough
sessions.bigIdea: Paul told the Corinthians to follow him as he followed Christ. He did not claim to have arrived. He claimed to be walking, and he invited people to walk behind him toward the same person. You do not need to be finished. You need to be moving.
sessions.open: Think of someone who helped your faith grow at some point. Were they a finished, perfect Christian, or just a bit further down the road than you? What did they actually give you?
sessions.read: Read 1 Corinthians 11:1. Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. One sentence. Paul, who called himself the foremost of sinners, tells ordinary believers to copy his life, and then he adds the safeguard. Only as far as he himself is copying Jesus.
observe: Paul says follow me, but he does not stop there. What is the condition he attaches? Where is the follower ultimately supposed to end up looking?
Paul never claims to have arrived. What does he claim instead? What is the posture the verse actually asks for?
talk: Discipling is not a perfect person handing down perfection. It is one person a few steps ahead saying, walk with me toward him. Who is a half step behind you right now that you have overlooked because you assumed you had nothing to give?

The as I am of Christ is the safety rail. You are not asking anyone to imitate you as the destination, only as an arrow pointing past you. How does that free you to invite someone along even while you are still a mess?

Being one step ahead means letting someone see your walk, including the stumbles. What is one honest thing about your own following of Jesus, struggle included, that would actually help someone behind you more than a polished version would?
sessions.practice: Name one person who is a step behind you in faith, a newer believer, a curious friend, a younger relative. This week, invite them into one ordinary part of your walk. Read a chapter together, pray once together, or just tell them what God has been doing in you.
sessions.send: You do not have to have arrived. You have to be walking. Turn around and see who is ready to walk behind you.
sessions.passItOn: Say to that person, plainly, I am not ahead of you by much, but you are welcome to walk with me toward Jesus. Those words, spoken out loud to a real name, are how the whole chain of following gets started again.

sessions.title: What If They Ask Something I Cannot Answer
sessions.bigIdea: Peter tells you to be ready to give a reason for your hope, and in the same breath he tells you to do it with gentleness and respect. He never tells you to have every answer. The freedom is in three honest words. I do not know, and let us find out together.
sessions.open: What is the hard question you are secretly afraid someone will ask you about God, the one that keeps you from starting the conversation at all? Name it out loud right now.
sessions.read: Read 1 Peter 3:15. But in your hearts honor Christ the Lord as holy, always being prepared to make a defense to anyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you, yet do it with gentleness and respect. Peter is writing to ordinary, scattered, pressured believers, not scholars, and he sets the bar at a reason for your hope, not a defense of every mystery.
observe: What exactly are you told to be ready to give a reason for? Notice it is not every doctrine. It is one specific thing. What is it?
Peter attaches two words to how you answer. What are they, and how do they change the goal from winning to something else?
talk: The verse asks for a reason for your hope, which is your own story of why you still trust Jesus. You already have that. So why do we let the fear of the hardest theological question stop us from sharing the one thing no one can argue with, what he has done in us?
Gentleness and respect means the goal was never to win the argument. When you feel cornered by a question, what would change if you did not have to defend God so much as point to him and stay kind?

Practice the freedom out loud. Say the sentence, I do not know, that is a good question, let us find out together. How does saying it feel? Notice that honesty builds more trust than a bluffed answer ever could.
sessions.practice: This week, when you do not know an answer, refuse to fake it and refuse to hide. Say I do not know, let us find out together, and then actually go look, ask your pastor, open a study, and come back with what you found. Model that not knowing is safe.
sessions.send: You were never asked to have every answer. You were asked for the reason for your hope, said gently. That much you already carry.
sessions.passItOn: Teach one other nervous believer the three words that set you free. I do not know. Show them that honesty, not expertise, is what keeps a conversation alive. A tool this small travels fast.

sessions.title: Start Before You Feel Ready
sessions.bigIdea: Moses and Gideon both stood in front of a clear call and answered with a list of reasons they were the wrong person. God did not argue with their self assessment. He simply promised to go with them. Obedience comes before the feeling of being qualified, never after it.
sessions.open: When have you waited to feel ready before doing something God seemed to be asking, and the ready feeling just never came? What happened while you waited?
sessions.read: Read Exodus 4:10-12. Moses said to the LORD, Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue. Then the LORD said to him, Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak. Then read Judges 6:14-16. The LORD turned to Gideon and said, Go in this might of yours and save Israel from the hand of Midian. Do not I send you? And Gideon said, Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house. And the LORD said to him, But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man.
observe: List the excuses Moses and Gideon give. What are they each pointing at as the reason they cannot do it?
God never disputes that Moses is slow of speech or that Gideon is the least. So what does God offer instead of arguing with the excuse? Find the promise both men get.
talk: Moses pleads his weakness and Gideon pleads his smallness, and both are telling the truth. God does not deny the weakness. He answers I will be with you. How does that change what your own excuse is actually worth?

Notice that the feeling of readiness never arrives in either story. The command comes first, the going comes next, and the equipping comes while they walk. Where are you waiting for a confidence that was only ever going to show up after you obeyed?

Both men measured themselves and came up short, which sounds like humility but was really a refusal to trust the one sending them. What excuse are you dressing up as humility to avoid stepping toward the person God has put in front of you?
sessions.practice: This week, take one action toward discipling someone before you feel ready. Send the text, ask the coffee question, open the Bible with them. Do the thing first and let the readiness catch up on the way, the way it did for Moses and Gideon.
sessions.send: God never argued Moses out of his stutter or Gideon out of his smallness. He said I will be with you and told them to go. So go.
sessions.passItOn: Find the believer near you who keeps saying they are not ready, and tell them Moses said the same thing with a stutter and God sent him anyway. Then ask them what one step they will take this week, and check back. Sometimes people just need one voice refusing to accept the excuse.

sessions.title: The Only Requirement
sessions.bigIdea: The great commission was given to a group of ordinary disciples, and some of them were still doubting when he gave it. The only requirements are a life going somewhere and one person you are willing to walk with, because the authority and the presence belong to him, not to you.
sessions.open: Six sessions in, what has actually changed about the excuse you started with? Say plainly where you still feel unqualified and where that grip has loosened.
sessions.read: Read Matthew 28:18-20. And Jesus came and said to them, All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age. Remember that Matthew said just before this that some of them doubted, and Jesus commissioned the doubters anyway.
observe: The command in the middle is make disciples, but it is bracketed by two promises. What is the promise before the command, and what is the promise after it? Whose authority and whose presence carry the whole thing?
Matthew notes that some doubted even as they worshiped. Who exactly did Jesus hand this commission to? What does that do to the idea that you need to be sure of yourself first?
talk: All authority is his, and the presence is his. Make disciples sits between two things you do not have to supply. So what is genuinely left for you to bring? Name the small, real requirement that is actually yours.

He gave this to doubters. Not to a cleaned up inner circle, to the same ordinary followers who ran the night he was arrested. If the commission was always for doubters, what is your last remaining reason to think it was not meant for you?

This is the last session, so it has to become a name, not a concept. Who is the one person you are willing to walk with, starting now? Say the name out loud, and say the first step you will take this week to begin.
sessions.practice: Before you leave this session, write down one name and one first step, and put a day on it. This week, take that step. Not a plan to disciple someone someday, a real action toward a real person now, with him going with you.
sessions.send: The authority is his. The presence is his. All he asked of you was to go and to bring one person along. You are qualified. Now go.
sessions.passItOn: You have just been discipled through six sessions. Do the whole thing again from the other chair. Take the person whose name you wrote down and walk them through this same study. That is how the doubters in Matthew 28 became the church, one ordinary person handing it to the next.
